about: The city in speech (Plato, Republic II-V, VIII): the founders' laws, the city's troubles, and the names of its people. Socrates' lines are close paraphrases with their Stephanus numbers; the troubles are the ones Athens lived through (Thucydides, Xenophon).

stages.name: The bare site
stages.goal: Pass the first law, and give each of the four first trades (farmer, builder, weaver, cobbler) one worker.

stages.name: The city of pigs
stages.goal: A healthy city, Socrates says. Glaucon calls it a city of pigs. Admit the luxuries to see how injustice grows.

stages.name: The fevered city
stages.goal: Luxury needs land. Take the neighbours' land, and raise an army of at least two to hold it.

stages.name: The army
stages.goal: Soldiers must be gentle to their own and fierce to strangers. Educate them, tell the story of the metals, forbid them gold, and choose at least two rulers.

stages.name: The guardians
stages.goal: Let philosophers rule, and put every person in the order their soul fits, until justice is at least 80 and unity at least 50.

stages.name: The just city
stages.goal: Each does their own work. Turn the city round and see your soul in it. Then, if you will, let the generations pass.

stages.name: Timocracy
stages.goal: The marriage number was missed. Honour rules now, and the soldiers love victory more than wisdom.

stages.name: Oligarchy
stages.goal: Wealth rules. The city is two cities, the rich and the poor, plotting against each other.

stages.name: Democracy
stages.goal: Freedom rules, and every desire is equal to every other. The city is full of every kind of person.

stages.name: Tyranny
stages.goal: The people's champion asked for a bodyguard and became a wolf. The worst city, and the most wretched soul.

laws.name: One person, one work
laws.socrates: We are not born alike: each is fit for one work. More is done, and better, when each does one thing, at the right time (370a-c).

laws.name: Admit the luxuries
laws.objection: Glaucon: If you were founding a city of pigs, Socrates, what else would you feed them? (372d)
laws.socrates: Very well: a fevered city. Perhaps in it we shall see how justice and injustice grow (372e).

laws.name: Take the neighbours' land
laws.socrates: We have found where war comes from: from the same desires that bring most of the evils to cities (373d-e).

laws.name: Music and gymnastics
laws.socrates: Music for the soul and gymnastics for the body, so the guardians are gentle to their own and fierce to strangers, like good dogs (375a-376e).

laws.name: Only good gods in the stories
laws.objection: Adeimantus: Then Homer himself must be sent away? (377d-e)
laws.socrates: The god is the cause of good things only. The young must not hear of gods who quarrel, lie and change their shapes (379c, 380d).

laws.name: The story of the metals
laws.socrates: Tell them they were made in the earth, all brothers, with gold mixed in the rulers, silver in the soldiers, bronze and iron in the rest (414b-415c).

laws.name: No gold for the guardians
laws.objection: Adeimantus: You will not make them very happy, Socrates. (419a)
laws.socrates: We are not making one class happy but the whole city. Let them eat together and handle no gold (416d-421c).

laws.name: Women guard and rule too
laws.socrates: The same nature fits the same work, and should have the same training. Women may be guardians (451d-457b).

laws.name: Marriage by lot, children in common
laws.objection: Glaucon: This wave is bigger than the last. (457c)
laws.socrates: The lots are arranged so the best have the most children, and no one knows their own; all call each other kin (458c-461e).

laws.name: Philosophers shall rule
laws.objection: Glaucon: Many will come at you, Socrates, with every weapon they can find. (473e-474a)
laws.socrates: Until philosophers rule as kings, or kings love wisdom, there will be no end of troubles for cities (473c-d).

events.title: A perfumer at the gate
events.text: A seller of perfumes and incense asks to settle in the city, with his couches and his cakes.

choices.socrates: And after him the painters, the cooks, the doctors. We shall need more land.
A healthy city, then, for now.

events.title: Plague
events.text: A sickness comes in with the grain ships. The people crowd inside the walls, and the dying lie in the streets (as at Athens, 430 BC).

choices.text: Close the gates and nurse the sick
choices.socrates: A city is a body too, and a sick body needs its doctor.
Then the city will learn what it values, one funeral at a time.

events.title: The grain ships are stopped
events.text: An enemy fleet sits in the strait. No grain comes by sea (as at Athens, 405 BC).

choices.socrates: Hunger shared is easier than hunger for some.
Now there are two cities inside the one wall.

events.title: The neighbours march
events.text: The neighbours want your land, as you wanted theirs.

choices.socrates: Now we see why the city needs guardians trained for nothing else.
Bought peace is rented, not owned.

events.title: Two cities in one
events.text: The rich and the poor no longer trust each other. There is talk of knives in the night (as at Corcyra, 427 BC).

choices.socrates: Wealth and poverty both ruin craftsmen; keep both out of the city (421d-422a).
Then it is not one city but two, at war with each other (422e-423a).

events.title: A plot of the few
events.text: A few rich men mean to seize the city and rule it for themselves (as the Four Hundred did at Athens, 411 BC).

choices.socrates: The guardians guard against enemies inside as well as outside (415d-e).
Men who rule for gain make the worst rulers.

events.title: A champion asks for a bodyguard
events.text: A popular leader says the rich want him dead, and asks the people for armed men to protect him.

choices.socrates: That is the famous request of every tyrant (566b). The wolf is at the door.
Good. A protector who needs an army against his own people is no protector.

events.title: The Great King's gold
events.text: An envoy of the King of Persia offers gold for your friendship, as he paid Sparta's fleet.

choices.socrates: Gold in the city finds its way into the guardians' hands.
A city that needs no one's gold can be no one's servant.

events.title: A guardian with a hoard
events.text: One of the rulers is found with gold hidden under his floor. He says everyone has some.

choices.text: Forbid gold to all the guardians
choices.socrates: Once they own land and houses and gold, they will be masters and enemies instead of allies (417a-b).
Then the shepherd's dogs are becoming wolves.

events.title: A poet at the gate
events.text: A poet arrives who can imitate anything at all, and offers to recite Homer, gods and all.

choices.text: Anoint him, crown him with wool, and send him on
choices.socrates: We honour him as a wonderful and holy man, and send him to another city (398a).
Then the children will learn that the gods quarrel, and think it no shame to quarrel themselves.

births: Children are mostly like their parents, but a golden child may be born to silver or bronze, and a bronze child to gold (415a-c).
